podcast.title: 2000 Chart Presence
podcast.body: Primitive Radio Gods were included in a list of bands that appeared on the charts in 2000, exemplifying the widespread belief that many rock and alt-rock acts were producing only one or two good songs over their entire careers. "If you look at the charts for 2000, we have bands like Mest, Eve 6, Fuel, Oliander, Lifhouse, Primitive Radio Gods, the Presidents of the United States of America."

podcast.title: Desperation Mailing of Demos
podcast.body: In 1994, Chris O'Connor, having decided to quit music, discovered a box of old demos while cleaning his house. In a "total desperation move," he mailed cassettes of these demos to every major label he could think of, not expecting any response. "In 1994, Chris was cleaning up around the house and found this box of demos."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Great Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders of the 90s: Part 2

podcast.title: Dropped by Label
podcast.body: Primitive Radio Gods were dropped by Fiction Records after their chosen follow-up single, "Mother Effor," failed due to its unpromotable title, which severely limited radio airplay. Despite this, the band continued to produce music independently. "And because nothing happened, surprise, they were dropped by their label."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Great Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders of the 90s: Part 2

podcast.title: Signing with Fiction Records
podcast.body: Weeks after O'Connor's desperate demo mailing, Fiction Records contacted him, expressing interest in his track "Standing Outside a Broken Phone Booth with Money in My Hand." The track's sample-based nature aligned with a growing trend in music, leading to his signing. "Until many weeks later, when he got a call from fiction records, they had liked this track called Standing Outside a Broken Phone Booth with Money in My Hand."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Great Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders of the 90s: Part 2

podcast.title: Solo Endeavor and Demos
podcast.body: After the breakup of his previous band, The I-Rails, singer Chris O'Connor began recording Public Enemy-inspired material under the name Primitive Radio Gods. He initially received no interest from radio or the music industry for these demos and decided to retire from music in 1994. "The band broke up, and singer Chris O'Connor went out on his own, recording some public enemy-inspired material under the name Primitive Radio Gods."

xref.title: The Cable Guy Soundtrack Contribution (1996)
xref.body: Silverchair contributed to *The Cable Guy* soundtrack in 1996, an album associated with the "creepy Jim Carrey vehicle" film. The soundtrack also featured other artists like Jerry Cantrell of Alice in Chains, Porno for Pyros, and Cracker. "Silver Chair Jerry Cantrell of Allyson Chains, Porno for Pyrrho's Cracker, and primitive radio gods ended up with a hit with standing outside a broken phone booth with money in my hand."

xref.title: 2000 Chart Presence
xref.body: Eve 6 was cited as one of the bands on the charts in 2000 that, in the perception of some rock fans, offered only a limited number of strong songs across their discography, contributing to a general dissatisfaction with the state of rock. "If you look at the charts for 2000, we have bands like Mest, Eve 6, Fuel, Oliander, Lifhouse, Primitive Radio Gods, the Presidents of the United States of America."

xref.title: 2000 Chart Presence
xref.body: Oleander was mentioned as a band charting in 2000, indicative of a period where rock acts were frequently perceived as offering only one to three good songs across several albums, leading to frustration among music fans. "If you look at the charts for 2000, we have bands like Mest, Eve 6, Fuel, Oliander, Lifhouse, Primitive Radio Gods, the Presidents of the United States of America."

xref.title: Influence on Chris O'Connor
xref.body: Chris O'Connor, the frontman for Primitive Radio Gods, was inspired by Public Enemy, incorporating elements of their style into his early solo material. This influence was evident in the demos he recorded under the Primitive Radio Gods name. "The band broke up, and singer Chris O'Connor went out on his own, recording some public enemy-inspired material under the name Primitive Radio Gods."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Great Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders of the 90s: Part 2

xref.title: Predecessor to Primitive Radio Gods
xref.body: The I-Rails was a Southern California band from which Primitive Radio Gods frontman Chris O'Connor evolved. Despite releasing four albums between 1985 and 1991, the band achieved no significant success and eventually broke up. "They evolved out of a Southern California band called the I-Rails, a group that amounted to exactly nothing over four albums between 1985 and 1991."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Great Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders of the 90s: Part 2

xref.title: Reunion for Primitive Radio Gods Tour
xref.body: When Primitive Radio Gods' single "Standing Outside a Broken Phone Booth with Money in My Hand" took off, singer Chris O'Connor reunited his former bandmates from The I-Rails to go on tour as Primitive Radio Gods. "When the song took off, singer Chris O'Connor got his old mates and the I-Rails back together and went on tour."
